title: [B1 • Band 5.0] Bài 117: The Dodo: Re-evaluating an Extinct Icon
passageHtml:
PASSAGE 117 (LEVEL B1 • BAND 5.0)

The Dodo: Re-evaluating an Extinct Icon

Paragraph 1. For more than three centuries, popular stories described the dodo as an oversized, clumsy, and foolish bird doomed by its own body. However, modern science and high-resolution bone scanning have completely overturned this Victorian myth. New evidence shows that the dodo was actually an active, muscular creature perfectly suited to its isolated island ecosystem.

Paragraph 2. Found exclusively on the volcanic island of Mauritius in the Indian Ocean, the dodo evolved from ancient fruit-eating pigeons that arrived about twenty-six million years ago. Because the island had zero land predators, losing the ability to fly saved huge amounts of energy. The bird developed strong leg bones and thick toe pads for running across rough forest paths, while a heavy, hooked beak helped it defend itself and crack hard forest nuts. Brain scans also reveal that the dodo's brain size matched that of modern pigeons, supported by an enlarged smell centre for locating fallen fruit.

Paragraph 3. The dodo's sudden disaster began in September 1598, when Dutch ships anchored at Mauritius for fresh food. Having evolved without ground enemies, dodos possessed a behaviour called island tameness, meaning they felt no instinctive fear of large strangers. Sailors could simply walk up and grab them by hand. Despite this easy capture, Dutch crews called it the 'disgusting bird' because its tough, oily meat required hours of boiling with cabbage just to become slightly edible.

Paragraph 4. Historical evidence proves that human hunting alone did not wipe out the species. The true catastrophe came from foreign mammals brought accidentally or intentionally by European ships, including pigs, black rats, dogs, and monkeys. Because dodos had never faced ground raiders, females laid only one large egg at a time in simple floor nests. While adult birds fought off humans bravely, pigs dug up eggs and rats devoured helpless chicks.

Paragraph 5. Within one hundred years of human arrival, the dodo vanished, with the final individuals likely dying around 1681. Sadly, European naturalists only realised the bird was extinct long after the last survivor had gone. True physical understanding remained hidden until 1865, when schoolteacher George Clark dug thousands of preserved bones from a wet Mauritian swamp, allowing modern researchers to build accurate digital models showing a surprisingly lean, upright runner.

groups.title: Questions 6–10
groups.instructions: Do the following statements agree with the information in the passage? Write TRUE, FALSE, or NOT GIVEN.

steps: Đoạn 2: "...a heavy, hooked beak helped it defend itself and crack hard forest nuts."
Đoạn 3: "...its tough, oily meat required hours of boiling..."
Đoạn 4: "...females laid only one large egg at a time..."
Đoạn 5: "...dug thousands of preserved bones from a wet Mauritian swamp..."

q6.text: The dodo had a much smaller brain for its body size than living pigeons.

steps: Đoạn 2: Kích thước não của dodo tương đương bồ câu hiện đại (matched that of modern pigeons).

q7.text: Dutch crews hunted dodos primarily to supply commercial meat markets in Europe.

steps: Đoạn 3: Thủy thủ bắt ăn tại chỗ nhưng chê thịt dở, không hề bán về châu Âu.

q8.text: Introduced animals such as pigs and monkeys played a greater role in extinction than hunting.

steps: Đoạn 4: Săn bắn không phải nguyên nhân chính; thảm họa thật sự đến từ thú ngoại lai trên tàu châu Âu.

q9.text: European scientists started a conservation project before the final dodos vanished.

steps: Đoạn 5: Giới khoa học chỉ nhận ra chim đã tuyệt chủng rất lâu sau khi con cuối cùng biến mất.

q10.text: George Clark was paid by the Mauritian government to drain the swamp in 1865.

steps: Đoạn 5: Chỉ nói thầy giáo George Clark đào được xương ở đầm lầy, không nhắc được chính phủ trả tiền rút nước.
